content: Lumbar puncture is a frequently performed invasive procedure in newborns, primarily for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes. However, approximately 50% of these procedures fail, which can lead to both immediate and long-term negative consequences for the clinical management of these patients. The two most commonly used positions for performing lumbar punctures are the lateral decubitus position and the sitting position, with each potentially influencing the success rate and safety of the procedure. Despite this, it remains unclear which position optimally improves patient outcomes. The objective of this review was to evaluate the benefits and risks associated with the lateral decubitus, sitting, and prone positions during lumbar puncture in newborn infants. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs involving newborns up to a postmenstrual age of 46 weeks and 0 days. The studies compared the outcomes of lumbar punctures performed in different positions. The primary outcomes assessed were the success of the lumbar puncture on the first attempt, the total number of attempts required, and the occurrence of bradycardia episodes. Standard Cochrane methods were used for data collection and analysis, and the GRADE approach was employed to evaluate the certainty of the evidence. Five studies involving a total of 1,476 participants were included in the review. When comparing the lateral decubitus position to the sitting position, the lateral decubitus position likely results in little to no difference in the success rate of lumbar puncture on the first attempt (low-certainty evidence). None of the studies reported the total number of lumbar puncture attempts. However, the lateral decubitus position was associated with an increased likelihood of bradycardia episodes (moderate-certainty evidence) and oxygen desaturation (moderate-certainty evidence). Specifically, the number needed to treat for an additional harmful outcome (NNTH) was 33 for bradycardia and 17 for oxygen desaturation. There was little to no difference in the time required to perform the lumbar puncture between the two positions (high-certainty evidence). Additionally, the lateral decubitus position may result in little to no difference in the number of apnea episodes during the procedure (low-certainty evidence). None of the studies reported the number of infants experiencing one or more episodes of apnea during the procedure. When comparing the lateral decubitus position to the prone position, the lateral decubitus position may reduce the success rate of lumbar puncture on the first attempt (low-certainty evidence). Only one study addressed this comparison, and it did not report on adverse effects. Pain intensity during and after the procedure was assessed using a non-validated pain scale, which introduces a high risk of bias. None of the studies comparing the lateral decubitus and prone positions reported on other critical outcomes specified in the review. In conclusion, when compared to the sitting position, the lateral decubitus position likely results in little to no difference in the success rate of lumbar puncture on the first attempt. However, the sitting position is associated with fewer episodes of bradycardia and oxygen desaturation. There is little to no difference in the time required to perform the procedure or in the number of apnea episodes between the two positions. When compared to the prone position, the lateral decubitus position may reduce the success rate of lumbar puncture on the first attempt, but the evidence is limited to a single study, and adverse effects were not evaluated. Most of the included studies involved term newborns, which limits the applicability of these findings to preterm infants. Further research using validated pain assessment tools and exploring the harms and benefits of different positions during lumbar puncture is needed to strengthen the confidence in these conclusions.
